prompt: Which of the four execution environments in this lesson has no screen a user ever looks at, and can only be reached by sending it a network request?
choices: Browser runtime
Desktop OS
Mobile OS
Cloud server

prompt: An iOS app tries to read another app's private files without asking for any permission. What actually stops it?
choices: The App Store reviewer manually checks for this in every submission
The operating system enforces a private per-app sandbox, so one app's container is invisible to another app
iOS apps are interpreted, so there's no way to access the filesystem at all
Nothing stops it — any app can read any other app's files on the same phone

prompt: A checkout page checks a promo code's format instantly in the browser with JavaScript, but a user opens DevTools, deletes that check, and sends the raw request straight to the API with curl. Where must the promo code actually be validated for the check to mean anything?
choices: In the browser's JavaScript, just written more carefully
In the HTML form itself
On the server, since it's the only code the user can't bypass or edit
In the browser's localStorage

prompt: In the C vs. Python vs. Node timing demo, the identical summing loop took about 0.14s in compiled C but about 3.4s in interpreted Python. What's the main reason for that gap?
choices: Python's loop runs on a slower CPU core by default
C's binary was already fully translated to machine code before running, while Python translates and executes the source through its interpreter every single run
Python doesn't support loops as efficiently as C syntactically
The Python version was actually computing a different, harder calculation

prompt: In that same demo, Node (JavaScript) finished the loop in about 0.07s — faster than the unoptimized C binary. What explains this?
choices: Node pre-compiles all JavaScript to a binary before the script is ever run, just like gcc does
JavaScript is a simpler language than C, so it needs fewer instructions
V8's JIT compiler detected the loop was 'hot' (run millions of times) and compiled just that code to machine code while the program was still running
The timing was inaccurate because Node doesn't actually execute real code

prompt: Which distribution channel has essentially no review gate before new code reaches anyone, but also the narrowest realistic reach, since users need a terminal and the right runtime already installed?
choices: App store (Apple App Store / Google Play)
Web distribution (a URL)
Package manager (npm, Homebrew, apt)
Enterprise device management

prompt: A team needs a critical bug fix live for 100% of their users within minutes, with no waiting on anyone else's approval. Which distribution model actually gets them there fastest?
choices: Submitting an emergency app store update and requesting expedited review
Publishing a new package manager version and asking users to update
Deploying the fix behind their existing web URL
Waiting for the next scheduled app store review cycle
